hero.title: SELECTED WORK
hero.lead: A selection of product work, direct client projects and collaborations across design and UI engineering. Explore the challenges, decisions and work behind each project.

picsart.title: Picsart
description: Worked across Picsart’s Growth and Marketplace teams on production UI for picsart.com and related product surfaces.
In Growth, I worked on scalable front-end UI, responsive behavior, accessibility and performance, including optimizations to Discovery pages.

Later, in Marketplace, I was a key Design System integration contributor for my team: bringing in shared components, building product-specific UI, and implementing multilingual RTL/LTR support within my scope.
This period shaped a lot of how I think about UI today: design systems, accessibility, localization and production quality all have to work together.

smartbet.title: Smartbet
description: Worked with Smartbet’s design and development team as UI Developer, turning approved layouts into an animated, responsive website.
I implemented the UI across every page, created a reusable atomic/BEM-based SCSS structure with design tokens, and wrote the JavaScript animations and transitions between pages and product sections.
A focused implementation role where precision, clean structure and collaboration with designers mattered most.

soulone.title: SoulOne
description: SoulOne is an Armenian bakery making gluten-free cakes and dessert balls, already supplying several cafés when I joined.

As Web Designer and Product Owner, I developed the visual direction — colours, typography and tone of voice — and designed an e-commerce website concept with interactive Figma prototypes, website copy and social media visuals.
The owner approved the design and brand direction, but the website was not developed or launched. The work brought together branding, product communication and interactive prototyping.

ginosi.title: Ginosi Apartels & Hotels
description: I built the full website front end for Ginosi, an international serviced-apartment and hospitality business, from the supplied design.
The work covered the booking experience, apartment listings, search and property interfaces, delivered within a tight schedule.

brainstorm.title: Brainstorm
description: My relationship with Brainstorm started with an outsourced assignment: building the agency’s own website while its design was still being developed.
I built the front end in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with custom animation and hand-written scroll-driven interactions.
The project led Brainstorm to invite me onto its team; this case focuses on the original website.

benzeen.title: Benzeen Auto Parts
description: Worked on Benzeen Auto Parts, a Los Angeles automotive e-commerce project delivered through TCO.
I built the site’s UI in Angular, HTML and SCSS/BEM, including responsive layouts, animations and selected JavaScript logic. I also implemented Google AMP; the project did not use a CMS.
Designers kept adding and updating pages during development, so design and implementation moved forward together.

worldEducation.title: World Education
description: I developed the website UI for World Education, a platform connecting students, schools, parents, agents, teachers and service providers around education opportunities.
I built most of the front end, including responsive layouts, animations and interactions; part of the JavaScript logic was handled by another developer.
It was a straightforward delivery project, showing end-to-end ownership of the site’s presentation layer.

sections.title: Who is responsible
body: Stepan Torchyan, an individual based in Yerevan, Armenia, operates Torchyan and is responsible for the personal data described in this notice.
Contact for anything about your data: hello@torchyan.design.

sections.title: What we collect
body: We collect the name, work email and message you submit, plus any optional details you provide, such as your company, website or product link, project type and timeline.
Standard technical data needed to deliver the website, such as your browser type and the pages requested.
When you send a message, your IP address is checked briefly in server memory to limit repeated submissions. It is not saved with your message.

sections.title: Why we use it
body: To reply to your enquiry and to take the steps you ask for before any agreement. Your details are not used for marketing and are not sold.

sections.title: Cookies and analytics
body: Vercel Web Analytics measures visits in aggregate. It does not use cookies, and visitors are identified only by a temporary hash that is discarded after 24 hours. The site does not use Google Analytics or Yandex Metrica.

The site sets one functional cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, which remembers your language choice (en, ru or hy) for one year. The language is first chosen from the country your request comes from, and only the language code is stored. The cookie does not identify you and is not used for tracking.

sections.title: Who processes it
body: Vercel hosts the website and provides analytics. Resend delivers contact-form submissions to a Gmail inbox provided by Google. ImprovMX forwards emails sent to hello@torchyan.design to the same inbox.
Some of these providers operate outside Armenia, including in the United States, so your data may be processed there.

sections.title: How long we keep it
body: Enquiries are kept for up to 24 months after our last contact, unless the law requires a longer period, and are then deleted.

sections.title: Your rights
body: You can ask to see, correct or delete the data you sent, or object to its use, by writing to hello@torchyan.design. You can also complain to your data protection authority.

sections.title: Changes
body: If this notice changes, the date above changes with it.

hero.title: A decade between design and code
hero.intro: I’m <name>Stepan Torchyan</name> — a designer, UI engineer and founder of Torchyan, based in Armenia. I work on websites, digital products and interface systems, connecting design decisions with how things are built.
hero.execution: That’s how I approach Torchyan too: design and development should work as one process, not two disconnected stages. I stay involved from the first idea through implementation, bringing in trusted specialists when the project needs them.
hero.resilience: At the end, the goal is simple: make things that look right, work well, and are built to last.

hero.subtitle: Growth & Marketplace - UI engineering at product scale
description: From October 2021 to February 2024, I worked as a Senior UI Engineer on picsart.com - first with the Growth team, then with Marketplace.
The work: integrating the Picsart Design System, building the components it didn’t cover, adding right-to-left language support from scratch, and a large part of the accessibility work in my scope.

timeline.title: What the work involved
subtitle: picsart.com is a large product surface, shipped by many teams at once.
My job was to keep the UI in my team’s scope consistent, accessible and ready for every language.

steps.title: Context
blocks: Picsart’s website serves many products and page types:
Marketing and business pages
Marketplace and Discovery
The editor and Mini Apps
Growth products such as Ad Wizard
Many teams ship to picsart.com at once. Each team has one person responsible for Design System integration - in my team’s scope, that was me.

steps.title: Growth team, 2021–2023
blocks: I was the team’s primary UI developer, focused on the Picsart website:
Modular, scalable UI in React, JSS and Styled Components
Responsive, cross-browser implementation
Accessibility work
Code reviews for performance, maintainability and best practice

steps.title: Ad Wizard
blocks: A separate Growth product where people create visual and social content and adapt it to the formats each platform needs - text, imagery, titles and emoji in one editor.
As the Growth team’s primary UI developer, I implemented its interface in React, HTML/CSS, JSS and Styled Components.

steps.title: Design System integration
blocks: I was the main UI and Design System integration owner for picsart.com and selected product branches in my team:
Integrated shared components across business pages, the editor and Mini Apps
Placed supplied components and templates as product required

steps.title: Components the system didn’t cover
blocks: The shared components came from the Design System team.
When a need wasn’t covered, I built the missing components for our product branch, matched to the system so the product still felt like one.

steps.title: Right-to-left languages
blocks: I implemented multilingual support, including RTL/LTR, from scratch for my scope.
Instead of fixing left and right values page by page, I reworked layout direction around logical properties - inline and block, start and end - so a change of direction carries through the structure.

steps.title: Accessibility
blocks: Accessibility was only minimally in place when I started. I handled a large part of the WCAG implementation work in my scope, building it into components rather than adding it afterwards.

steps.title: Responsive and cross-browser
blocks: Every component checked across breakpoints and browsers, so pages behaved the same for every visitor.

steps.title: Performance
blocks: On the Growth team, I optimized the Discovery pages and their codebase.
Pages were measured before and after; the figures aren’t published here.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: Right-to-left languages supported structurally, not by manual fixes
Marketplace pages consistent with the shared Design System
Accessibility built into components in my scope
Faster Discovery pages

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: Work at product scale, inside large teams and shared systems
Localization and accessibility treated as structure, not patches
The same standards applied to every Torchyan project

blueprint.title: Integration principles
blueprint.subtitle: How the shared Design System was carried into the pages in my scope.

cards.title: Shared first
cards.body: Use Design System components wherever they fit; build new ones only for real gaps.

cards.title: Match the system
cards.body: New components follow the shared tokens, spacing and states.

cards.title: Direction-agnostic layout
cards.body: Logical properties instead of left and right, so RTL works structurally.

cards.title: Accessible by default
cards.body: Accessibility considered in every component, not added later.

cards.title: Responsive everywhere
cards.body: Every component checked across breakpoints and browsers.

architecture.title: In detail
architecture.subtitle: Five parts of the work, and how each was approached.

useCases.title: 1. RTL/LTR layout logic
blocks: Switching a page between left-to-right and right-to-left usually means hunting down every left and right value.
I rebuilt the layout direction around logical properties:
margin-inline and padding-inline instead of left and right
inset-inline-start and inset-inline-end for positioning
Direction set once, at the root
A direction change now carries through the structure instead of being patched page by page.

useCases.title: 2. Design System integration
blocks: Shared components from the Design System team, integrated across:
Business and product pages
The editor
Mini Apps
Placement followed product direction; consistency across branches was my responsibility in my team’s scope.

useCases.title: 3. Components the system didn’t cover
blocks: Some Marketplace needs weren’t in the shared system. For those, I built team-specific components that:
Use the shared tokens
Follow the same states and spacing
Stay responsive and accessible

useCases.title: 4. Accessibility implementation
blocks: From a minimal starting point, accessibility became part of the components in my scope rather than a late fix. I handled a large part of that WCAG implementation work myself.

useCases.title: 5. Ad Wizard
blocks: A separate Growth product for creating visual and social content and adapting it to each platform’s formats. As the team’s primary UI developer, I implemented its interface in React, HTML/CSS, JSS and Styled Components.

hero.title: Smartbet
hero.subtitle: An animated company and product website - sports, gaming, platform products and services
description: From August to October 2021, I worked as a UI Developer at Smartbet, in a team of designers and developers. The design team supplied approved layouts; I implemented the UI for every page of the website, including the responsive versions.
Alongside the page builds, I set up a reusable atomic/BEM-based SCSS structure with styling tokens, and implemented the JavaScript animations and transitions between pages and product sections.

timeline.title: What the work involved
subtitle: Smartbet’s website presents distinct product families - sports, gaming and platform tools - alongside solutions, payment methods, providers and company pages.
The designs were approved; my job was to turn every page into working, responsive, animated UI.

steps.title: Context
blocks: Approved designs were ready for front-end implementation. The website covered:
Sports products
Gaming products
Platform tools
Solutions, payment methods and providers
Company pages

steps.title: A UI foundation
blocks: A reusable SCSS structure, organised with atomic/BEM naming and styling tokens, so every page drew on the same rules.

steps.title: Product pages
blocks: Every approved layout implemented across the sports, gaming and platform categories.
Each product family has its own visual theme, inside one consistent site structure.

steps.title: Motion
blocks: JavaScript animations and transitions that move titles, imagery and coloured section accents together as visitors go from page to page and product to product.

steps.title: Supporting sections, on every screen
blocks: Services, solutions, providers, payment methods and company pages, their content entering in stages.
Every page adapted across screen sizes, with navigation, typography and UI patterns kept aligned.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: The UI implemented across every page of the website
Animated page states and transitions between product families
One reusable styling foundation for the whole site

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: End-to-end responsibility for the website UI - not the backend or the product design
A reusable styling foundation alongside motion-heavy implementation
Accurate collaboration with a design team on a visually complex, multi-section site

blueprint.title: Principles
blueprint.subtitle: What the build held to, page after page.

cards.title: Design fidelity
cards.body: Approved layouts translated accurately into working pages.

cards.title: Reusability
cards.body: Atomic/BEM-based styling and tokens, shared by every page.

cards.title: Consistent motion
cards.body: Transitions that stay coherent across product families.

cards.title: Responsive structure
cards.body: The same experience, preserved across screen sizes.

cards.title: Visual consistency
cards.body: Navigation, typography and UI patterns kept aligned.

architecture.title: In detail
architecture.subtitle: Five parts of the build, and how each was approached.

useCases.title: 1. Moving between products
blocks: Going from one product to another changes titles, imagery and coloured section accents at once.
I implemented those transitions in JavaScript, so incoming and outgoing content hand over in step.

useCases.title: 2. Different product identities
blocks: Sports, gaming and platform sections each carry their own visual theme.
They share one site structure, so navigation and layout stay familiar while colour and imagery change.

useCases.title: 3. A hero in motion
blocks: The homepage opens on a continuously moving, shape-changing visual object, set alongside the hero content.

useCases.title: 4. The navigation overlay
blocks: A full-page menu, grouped by product category, that opens and closes as an animated state.

useCases.title: 5. Staged content
blocks: Service illustrations, support details, and the provider and payment grids enter progressively rather than all at once.

hero.title: SoulOne
hero.subtitle: Brand direction and an interactive e-commerce website concept for an Armenian gluten-free bakery
description: From May to October 2025, I worked with SoulOne as Web Designer and Product Owner, as part of its founding team. The bakery was already making gluten-free cakes and dessert balls and supplying several cafés.

I designed the website and its interactive Figma prototypes, and set the colour palette, typography, tone of voice, website copy and social-media visuals. The website stayed a concept: it was not built or launched, and the business later stopped trading.

meta.label: Team:
items: Founding team, with the bakery’s owner

timeline.title: What the work involved
subtitle: SoulOne already had products and customers.
It needed a coherent identity, a clear voice and an online presentation to match.

steps.title: Context
blocks: An existing bakery - not a business started from zero - with gluten-free cakes and dessert balls already supplied to cafés.
The task: a more coherent visual identity, tone of voice and online product presentation, and a website concept.

steps.title: Brand foundations
blocks: Tone of voice, colour palette and typography, set first so every later screen and post drew on them.

steps.title: Messaging
blocks: Website messaging and product copy, written in that voice.

steps.title: The homepage
blocks: Product ranges, the brand story, product benefits and calls to action.
Cakes and dessert balls side by side, with a Build Your Box concept.

steps.title: Product pages
blocks: Detail views with imagery, price, quantities, ingredients, nutrition and allergens, and related products.

steps.title: Prototype and social
blocks: Interactive Figma prototypes for product image states and transitions, and visuals for social media.
An alternative logo was explored too; the original logo was kept.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: A visual direction: palette, typography and tone of voice
A complete website UI concept, with interactive prototypes
Website copy and social creative
The website itself was not built or launched, so there are no sales or conversion figures to report.

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: Range beyond screens: brand direction, UX/UI, product communication and prototyping
Product involvement in an existing business, not only its visuals

blueprint.title: What the designs prioritise
blueprint.subtitle: The choices that run through the concept.

cards.title: Food first
cards.body: Photography of the cakes leads every page.

cards.title: An easy range
cards.body: Cakes and dessert balls stay simple to browse.

cards.title: Details in reach
cards.body: Ingredients and product details are easy to find.

cards.title: One voice
cards.body: Colour, typography and tone stay consistent.

cards.title: Shown, not described
cards.body: Commerce interactions are visible in the prototype.

architecture.title: In detail
architecture.subtitle: Design problems, and the solutions the concept proposes.

useCases.title: 1. A disconnected brand
blocks: The bakery’s presentation didn’t hang together.
A defined palette, typography and tone of voice gave every touchpoint the same footing.

useCases.title: 2. Two ranges, one shop
blocks: Cakes and dessert balls needed to sit side by side.
Structured homepage and product sections, and a Build Your Box concept, bring them together.

useCases.title: 3. Explaining each product
blocks: Detailed product pages with imagery, price, ingredients, allergens and related items.

useCases.title: 4. Interactions before development
blocks: Figma prototype states and transitions show how the site would behave, before any of it is built.

useCases.title: 5. The logo
blocks: I designed an alternative logo; the owner chose to keep the existing one.

hero.title: Ginosi
hero.subtitle: Full front-end implementation for an international serviced-apartment booking website
description: Ginosi offered serviced apartments in several cities and countries. Its website let visitors search for accommodation and reserve apartments.

Working directly with the client in April–May 2019, I joined when the visual design was already in place and implemented the full front end under a tight schedule - turning the supplied designs into the working booking-site UI.

timeline.title: What the work involved
subtitle: An established accommodation business, with its booking website already designed.
It needed all of it built as a working front end, quickly.

steps.title: Context
blocks: Ginosi’s visual design already existed. What it needed was a front end that worked.

steps.title: From designs to structure
blocks: The supplied designs reviewed, then turned into a shared layout and styling for every page.

steps.title: Search, listings and properties
blocks: The accommodation search, the listings and the property pages - the core of the booking experience.

steps.title: Every screen size
blocks: Responsive behaviour across the site, then the finished front end handed over.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: The entire front-end UI, delivered within a very short timeframe - sooner than the client had asked for.

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: End-to-end ownership of the presentation layer
Speed of execution
Implementing another designer’s work accurately

blueprint.title: Principles
blueprint.subtitle: What a fast build still held to.

cards.title: Faithful to the design
cards.body: The approved visual design, implemented as drawn.

cards.title: Consistent patterns
cards.body: Common patterns kept the same across every page.

cards.title: Reliable delivery
cards.body: A tight schedule, met without cutting corners.

cards.title: Every screen size
cards.body: An interface that works on every screen.

hero.title: Benzeen Auto Parts
hero.subtitle: UI and interaction engineering for a custom automotive e-commerce site, built alongside an evolving design
description: Benzeen Auto Parts was an automotive e-commerce project for a business in Los Angeles, delivered through TCO in 2019. Designers kept preparing and updating pages while development was underway.
I implemented the UI across the website - interactive behaviour, animations and selected JavaScript logic - and integrated Google AMP. It was my first e-commerce project outside a traditional CMS.

subtitle: A custom e-commerce build, not a CMS theme.
New page designs kept arriving while the site was being built.

steps.title: Context
blocks: A custom, non-CMS e-commerce build in Angular. Design updates and new page concepts arrived while development was already underway.

steps.title: Structure and shared styling
blocks: Page structure and shared styling first, written in Sass/SCSS with BEM.

steps.title: Alongside the designers
blocks: Pages implemented and updated as the designs changed, in step with the design team.

steps.title: The storefront
blocks: The UI across the whole store: browsing by make, recent arrivals, stock and part pages, quotes and the customer account.

steps.title: Interaction and AMP
blocks: Animations and JavaScript behaviour across the site, and Google AMP integrated for supported mobile content.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: The UI implemented across the site
Interactive behaviour and animations
Google AMP integrated

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: Full UI implementation for custom e-commerce
Close collaboration with designers while the design moved
Animation work, and experience with non-CMS Angular projects

blueprint.title: Principles
blueprint.subtitle: How the build kept up with a moving design.

cards.title: Stay aligned
cards.body: Design and implementation kept in step as requirements changed.

cards.title: Structured styling
cards.body: BEM and SCSS, so new pages fit the existing ones.

cards.title: Deliberate details
cards.body: Interaction details built with intention, not left to chance.

cards.title: One storefront
cards.body: A large product surface kept consistent throughout.

architecture.title: In detail
architecture.subtitle: Two parts of the work, and how each was approached.

useCases.title: 1. A design that kept changing
blocks: New pages were still being designed while the site was built.
Iterative implementation, on structured Sass/BEM patterns, let new and updated pages slot into what already existed.

useCases.title: 2. Google AMP
blocks: I integrated Google AMP into the project for the mobile content it supported, alongside the main Angular build.

hero.title: Brainstorm
hero.subtitle: Custom front-end and scroll-driven interaction work for Brainstorm’s agency website
description: It began in 2018 as an outsourced assignment: building Brainstorm’s own agency website while its design was still being developed.

I built the website UI in HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with custom animation and hand-written scroll-event logic. The finished site led Brainstorm to invite me onto its team, where I went on to work on client stores - those are separate projects.

timeline.title: What the work involved
subtitle: Brainstorm needed its own site built while the design was still taking shape.

steps.title: Context
blocks: The agency’s own website, with the design still being developed and refined as the front end was built.

steps.title: An evolving design
blocks: Working directly with the design as it changed, rather than waiting for a final version.

steps.title: Layouts and responsive UI
blocks: Every layout implemented and made responsive, in step with the visual concept.

steps.title: Custom animation
blocks: Animation built as part of the experience, not added on top of it.

steps.title: Scroll-triggered events
blocks: Scroll-driven events and transitions, coded by hand in JavaScript rather than taken from generic animation templates.

steps.title: What changed
blocks: An animated, custom front-end site for the agency
An invitation to join Brainstorm as a developer

steps.title: What this shows
blocks: Independent front-end delivery
Custom JavaScript motion, implemented by hand
A client engagement that grew into a longer working relationship

blueprint.title: Principles
blueprint.subtitle: How the site was built while its design was still moving.

cards.title: Work with the design
cards.body: Build directly against an evolving design.

cards.title: Motion with a job
cards.body: Animation as a working part of the experience.

cards.title: Explicit scrolling
cards.body: Scroll interactions controlled in code, not by templates.

cards.title: Responsive concept
cards.body: Responsive behaviour kept true to the visual idea.

architecture.title: In detail
architecture.subtitle: Two parts of the work, and how each was approached.

useCases.title: 1. Scroll-driven animation, by hand
blocks: The site’s animation and interactions are driven by scrolling.
Rather than relying on generic animation templates, I implemented the JavaScript event behaviour myself, so each page animates the way it was meant to.

useCases.title: 2. A design still taking shape
blocks: The designs were still evolving while the front end was underway.
Building in step with them meant the finished site matched the final design, not an early draft of it.

hero.title: World Education
hero.subtitle: Responsive UI implementation for an international education-services platform
description: World Education connects schools, agents, students, parents, teachers and service providers around education, university admissions, tests, guides and scholarship information.

Working directly with the client from March to May 2020, I built most of the website’s front end as UI Developer, including responsive layouts and animations; some of the JavaScript logic was handled by another contributor. The site still runs in much the same form.
